title: Adam momentum too high causes training instability
description: The default Adam momentum term of 0.9 resulted in training oscillation and instability; reducing it to 0.5 was needed to stabilize training.
canonical_description: default Adam momentum causes training oscillation and requires reduction

evidence.quote: Additionally, we found leaving the momentum term $\beta_1$ at the suggested value of 0.9 resulted in training oscillation and instability while reducing it to 0.5 helped stabilize training.

verdict.reasoning: Neither paper investigates the specific claim that default Adam momentum (β₁=0.9) causes oscillation/instability in GAN training and requires reduction to 0.5. Paper 1 (Optimistic Adam) addresses training oscillation through a different mechanism — an optimistic correction term — but uses β₁=0.5 throughout and never analyzes the effect of different momentum values nor compares Optimistic Adam at β₁=0.9 vs β₁=0.5. It thus sidesteps the gap's core question rather than answering it. Paper 2 (LADAM) focuses on learning-rate and batch-size adaptation, never mentions momentum at all. The gap — whether the default Adam momentum itself is the cause and whether reducing it is the appropriate fix — remains completely unexamined by both papers.

paper.title: Training GANs with Optimism
paper.abstract: We address the issue of limit cycling behavior in training Generative Adversarial Networks and propose the use of Optimistic Mirror Decent (OMD) for training Wasserstein GANs. Recent theoretical results have shown that optimistic mirror decent (OMD) can enjoy faster regret rates in the context of zero-sum games. WGANs is exactly a context of solving a zero-sum game with simultaneous no-regret dynamics. Moreover, we show that optimistic mirror decent addresses the limit cycling problem in training WGANs. We formally show that in the case of bi-linear zero-sum games the last iterate of OMD dynamics converges to an equilibrium, in contrast to GD dynamics which are bound to cycle. We also portray the huge qualitative difference between GD and OMD dynamics with toy examples, even when GD is modified with many adaptations proposed in the recent literature, such as gradient penalty or momentum. We apply OMD WGAN training to a bioinformatics problem of generating DNA sequences. We observe that models trained with OMD achieve consistently smaller KL divergence with respect to the true underlying distribution, than models trained with GD variants. Finally, we introduce a new algorithm, Optimistic Adam, which is an optimistic variant of Adam. We apply it to WGAN training on CIFAR10 and observe improved performance in terms of inception score as compared to Adam.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Optimistic Adam, a variant of Adam that adds an optimistic correction term (using the previous gradient as a predictor) to address limit cycling and instability in GAN training. It shows theoretically that Optimistic Mirror Descent converges in last-iterate for bilinear games (where GD diverges/cycles), and empirically demonstrates that Optimistic Adam achieves better inception scores on CIFAR10 and lower KL divergence on DNA sequence generation compared to standard Adam. The paper addresses the same symptom described in the gap (training oscillation/instability) but through a different mechanism — modifying the update rule with optimism rather than tuning the momentum parameter.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the specific problem stated in the gap: that the default Adam momentum of 0.9 causes instability and needs to be reduced to 0.5. The paper uses β₁=0.5 throughout (matching Gulrajani et al. 2017) for both Adam and Optimistic Adam, and never analyzes the effect of different momentum values or compares Optimistic Adam's behavior at β₁=0.9 vs β₁=0.5. The gap's specific question — whether the momentum term itself is the cause of instability and whether reducing it is the right fix — remains unanswered. The paper proposes an orthogonal fix (optimism) that works at β₁=0.5 but doesn't investigate whether it would also stabilize training at β₁=0.9, nor does it compare against simply reducing momentum as a baseline.
evidence_snippets: We trained on CIFAR10 images with Optimistic Adam with the hyper-parameters matched to [CITE:Gulrajani2017], and we observe that it outperforms Adam in terms of inception score
The same learning rate $0.0001$ and betas ($\beta_1=0.5, \beta_2=0.9$) as in Appendix B of [CITE:Gulrajani2017]  were used for all the methods compared.
We apply it to WGAN training on CIFAR10 and observe improved performance in terms of inception score as compared to Adam.

paper.title: Convergence of GANs Training: A Game and Stochastic Control Methodology
paper.abstract: Training generative adversarial networks (GANs) is known to be difficult, especially for financial time series. This paper first analyzes the well-posedness problem in GANs minimax games and the convexity issue in GANs objective functions. It then proposes a stochastic control framework for hyper-parameters tuning in GANs training. The weak form of dynamic programming principle and the uniqueness and the existence of the value function in the viscosity sense for the corresponding minimax game are established. In particular, explicit forms for the optimal adaptive learning rate and batch size are derived and are shown to depend on the convexity of the objective function, revealing a relation between improper choices of learning rate and explosion in GANs training. Finally, empirical studies demonstrate that training algorithms incorporating this adaptive control approach outperform the standard ADAM method in terms of convergence and robustness. From GANs training perspective, the analysis in this paper provides analytical support for the popular practice of ``clipping'', and suggests that the convexity and well-posedness issues in GANs may be tackled through appropriate choices of hyper-parameters.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes a stochastic control framework for tuning hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, time scale) in GANs training. It derives optimal adaptive learning rates and batch sizes based on convexity of the objective function, and introduces LADAM (an adaptive learning rate variant of ADAM). The paper shows that LADAM outperforms standard ADAM in terms of convergence speed and robustness for GANs training on synthetic and financial time series data.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the specific gap about Adam's momentum parameter (β₁). The gap concerns the default Adam momentum of 0.9 causing training oscillation/instability, requiring reduction to 0.5. This paper focuses entirely on learning rate adaptation and batch size control, not on momentum. The momentum parameter of Adam (β₁) is never mentioned, analyzed, or modified anywhere in the paper. The instability it addresses is from improper learning rates (explosion), not from momentum-induced oscillation.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The gap is a focused hyperparameter-ablation question — does default Adam β₁=0.9 cause oscillation, and does reducing to 0.5 fix it? This is highly tractable: (1) Data is abundant (standard GAN datasets: CIFAR, CelebA, LSUN). (2) Compute is modest — small-to-medium GANs (DCGAN, WGAN-GP) train on a single GPU; no frontier-scale training needed. (3) Methodological maturity is high — systematic variation of β₁ while holding other hyperparameters fixed is a straightforward experimental design; tools (PyTorch/TensorFlow, FID/IS metrics, loss-curve analysis) are off-the-shelf. (4) Scope is narrow and well-defined — not an open-ended research agenda. (5) Evaluability is strong — training stability is measurable via FID scores, loss oscillation amplitude, gradient-norm variance, and replication across random seeds. The main challenge is that GAN training is stochastic and sensitive to architecture/dataset choices, so careful controls and multiple seeds are needed to isolate the momentum effect. But no fundamental breakthrough is required.
